claims.text: Rapidly solidified high-entropy alloys can contain a largely disordered matrix with localized chemical inhomogeneities or incipient nanoclusters.
A short intermediate-temperature anneal enhances and stabilizes SRO nanoclusters.
A full homogenization treatment dissolves or significantly reduces SRO nanoclusters.
Nanoscale SRO clusters create local stress fields and impede dislocation motion.
At low strain rates, SRO clusters increase yield strength by obstructing dislocation motion.
At high strain rates, applied stress causes SRO clusters to dissolve or reconfigure.
Stress-driven cluster transformation releases stored dislocations or creates new mobile dislocation sources.
The additional dislocation sources delay strain localization and enhance ductility during high-rate loading.
The dual obstacle/source role of SRO clusters can reconcile high strength with high ductility.
Relative to a homogenized baseline, the SRO-enhanced alloy will have higher dynamic yield strength.
Relative to a homogenized baseline, the SRO-enhanced alloy will sustain greater plastic deformation under high-strain-rate loading.
The strength and ductility benefits of SRO clusters will be less pronounced under quasi-static loading than under dynamic loading.
A homogenized, cluster-reduced baseline will exhibit lower dynamic yield strength.
A homogenized, cluster-reduced baseline will exhibit less work hardening under high-strain-rate loading.
The proposed mechanism should operate from ambient to moderate temperatures while the nanoclusters remain thermally stable.
The mechanism may cease to apply at extremely high temperatures or strain rates where diffusion or melting effects dominate.
The hypothesis is rejected if the SRO-enhanced samples lack significantly higher dynamic yield strength and ductility, or if stress-assisted cluster transformation is not observed.
